question.text: The tax head of Silverline Capital is reviewing a proposed structure where an offshore Mauritius investor routes capital into an Indian Cat II AIF to invest in an Indian portfolio company. The arrangement's dominant purpose is to avoid Indian capital gains tax on the portfolio exit using the Mauritius treaty. Which ITA provision enables the tax authorities to disregard/recharacterise this structure?

answer.text: General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR), effective 1 April 2017 — applies if main purpose is tax benefit AND one of four tainted elements is met (non-arm's-length, misuse of ITA, lacks commercial substance, bona fide-unusual manner)

explanation.text: The Logic: GAAR is effective from 1 April 2017 and applies to impermissible avoidance arrangements where the main purpose is to obtain a tax benefit and at least one of four tainted elements is present: (a) rights/obligations not at arm's length, (b) misuse or abuse of the ITA, (c) lack of commercial substance, or (d) carried out in a manner not normally employed for bona fide purposes. Once invoked, the tax authorities are empowered to reallocate, re-characterise, or disregard the arrangement. The workbook also notes that a treaty's LOB clarification can interact with GAAR in specific cases. The Trap: Option B — Section 115UB sets out the pass-through mechanics for Cat I/II AIFs; it does not give a recharacterisation power. Option C — Section 56(2)(x) deals with receipt of property below FMV. Option D — Section 194LBB is a TDS provision on AIF distributions. Note: The provision being tested is GAAR's four-element framework and its recharacterisation power. The interaction with a particular treaty's LOB clarification can be raised separately if and only if it is sourced.
